questions.title: When a federal indictment is dismissed for failure to state an offense, why does the appellate court assume the alleged facts are true?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the procedure here. The district court dismissed the indictment before trial, but the Fifth Circuit says review is de novo and that it must take the indictment's allegations as true. Is the court only asking whether the indictment alleges every element of the offense, rather than whether the government can actually prove those allegations? If so, how is this different from reviewing evidentiary sufficiency after trial, and why is the government allowed to appeal this kind of pretrial dismissal?

questions.title: Why did the Fifth Circuit analyze Section 1348 securities fraud using mail and wire fraud cases instead of ordinary Rule 10b-5 doctrine?
questions.question_body: The opinion says there is scant caselaw on 18 U.S.C. Section 1348 in the Fifth Circuit, so it borrows the concepts of a scheme to defraud and intent to defraud from mail and wire fraud cases. I thought securities fraud usually involved concepts like reliance, loss causation, and the Rule 10b-5 line of cases. Is Section 1348 a different criminal statute with different elements? What exactly did the government have to allege here under Section 1348 and the conspiracy statute, Section 1349?

questions.title: Why wasn't this pump-and-dump indictment just a forbidden right-to-control theory under Ciminelli?
questions.question_body: The defendants argued that, at most, they deprived their followers of accurate market information about the defendants' own trading positions and intentions. That sounds a lot like depriving someone of valuable economic information, which Ciminelli said is not a traditional property interest. But the Fifth Circuit says this case is different because it alleges fraudulent inducement to buy securities. I'm having trouble seeing the line. If the lie only affected the investors' decision-making, why isn't this still just an information-deprivation theory in disguise?

questions.title: How is a victim deprived of money or property when they buy stock and receive stock in return?
questions.question_body: This is the part I find most counterintuitive. The followers allegedly paid money to buy securities because of the misleading posts, but they still got shares when they paid. The court says that is enough because they were induced by fraud to part with their money, even if they received market-value securities in exchange. How does that qualify as property fraud after Ciminelli? Doesn't fraud usually require that the victim lose the thing the defendant is trying to obtain?

questions.title: After Kousisis, does intent to defraud require intending to make the victim economically worse off?
questions.question_body: The defendants argued that they intended to profit from the scheme, not to injure their followers. The Fifth Circuit says that distinction does not matter because the object was to obtain money by deception. Does that mean criminal fraud no longer requires any intended economic harm at all, so long as the defendant lies to induce a transaction involving money or property? If actual or intended net loss is unnecessary, what is the limiting principle?

questions.title: For federal fraud, does the victim's money have to go directly to the defendant?
questions.question_body: In a pump-and-dump scheme, the deceived followers may be buying in the market from whoever happens to be selling, while the defendants profit by unloading their own shares into the inflated market. That seems less direct than a classic fraud where the victim hands money straight to the fraudster. The opinion cites Baker to say there is no mirror-image requirement between the victim's loss and the defendant's gain. How indirect can the transfer be before it stops counting as obtaining the victim's money or property by fraud?
